corrections.caveats: The README table reports each program's own 'Processing time (w/o IO)' (extract_results.dart pTimeRegex), and both cpp/main.cpp and c3/related.c3 start the clock after the JSON is parsed and stop it before the JSON is written, so JSON parsing (nlohmann/json vs the hand-written json.c3) is NOT in the measured numbers; it only shows in the wall-clock 'total' lines of the raw files (60k posts: C++ about 3.35 s, c3 about 1.76 s). The algorithm is the same on both sides (tag-to-post-index map, uint8 shared-tag counters, 64-byte chunk filter, insertion top-5), and C3 even does extra hashing (has_key/set/get_ref per tag when building the index and a map get per tag per post), while C++ resolves each tag's vector once. The main asymmetry is runtime checks: the C++ solution indexes with std::vector::at() in the counting and top-5 loops (bounds checks kept, as the suite's 'no disabling runtime checks' rule requires), while c3c -O3 turns safety checks off entirely, so the C3 build does not keep the bounds checks the rules ask for. C++ and c3 rows come from separate runs (results committed 2026-02-24 and 2026-02-11) on the same VM type; CPU model (c7a.xlarge) and clang version are not stated. Timers have 1 ms resolution on both sides, so the 5k-post margin (10.50 vs 12.20 ms) is near the timer granularity. Community-written implementations; no plain C solution.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Verifier reading of the code (not measured): c3c -O3 disables runtime safety checks, while the C++ baseline keeps std::vector::at() bounds checks in its hot counting and top-5 loops; C3 also allocates the per-run arrays from its temp arena. Codegen backend is LLVM on both sides (C3 at the O2 pipeline), so the win is most likely check elimination by build mode, not language codegen.

corrections.caveats: Margin is 9-16% and flips by benchmark: on mandel.b Rust is slower than every C and C++ row. All three are the same naive tree-walking interpreter (no run-length folding), but the op representations differ: Rust uses an enum with separate Inc/Dec variants and boxed child slices and reads the tape with unsafe get_unchecked, C uses a 16-byte tagged union with an offset field and a tape_get that truncates the int cell to char, and C++ uses a 32-byte Op struct that embeds a std::vector in every op. V/gcc, which emits C and compiles it with gcc, is faster than the C row, which points to data-layout and codegen variance rather than a language advantage. The suite reports median with median absolute deviation from a ~1 s run; no mechanism is given by the source.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Verifier reading of the code (not measured): equal build settings on both sides (O3-level, native CPU, full LTO, 32-byte branch alignment), and Rust uses unsafe get_unchecked so it pays no bounds checks either; the small bench.b lead most likely comes from the different op layouts (Rust enum with Inc/Dec variants vs C tagged union with an offset load and char-truncating tape_get, C++ Op with an embedded std::vector) and the resulting dispatch codegen, which mandel.b reverses.
